records.literal_gloss: And you, take up a lament for the princes of Israel,

en.L: And you, take up a lament for the princes of Israel,
en.B: And you, raise a lament over the princes of Israel,
en.R: Sing a funeral song for the rulers of Israel.

decisions.choice: a lament: a funeral song, here sung over the royal house of Judah
decisions.reason: A lament (*qinah*) was the song sung for the dead (2 Samuel 1:17-27). Most of its lines have a long half and a shorter half, a limping rhythm that suits grief; Lamentations is written in it. The prophets sometimes sang such a song over people who were still alive, to say that their end was certain (Amos 5:1-2). The chapter is set in lines as poetry.

decisions.choice: the princes of Israel: the last kings of Judah
decisions.reason: The lament is about two kings pictured as lion cubs (verses 2-9) and about the royal line pictured as a vine (verses 10-14). "Israel" here means the people of God, of whom Judah was all that was left. Ezekiel often calls Judah's kings "princes" (12:10; 21:30).

decisions.choice: and you: the LORD speaks to Ezekiel and gives him the lament to sing
decisions.reason: The chapter goes on from the LORD's words to Ezekiel in chapter 18, with no new heading. The whole lament is what Ezekiel is told to sing.

decisions.choice: no quotation marks, and the chapter set in lines
decisions.reason: The rule set for the prophets' poetry holds: the LORD's words to the prophet and the prophet's poems take no quotation marks. Verse 1 is a single line; the lament from verse 2 on follows the Hebrew accents for its line breaks.

decisions.choice: lament (L, B); funeral song (R); princes (L, B); rulers (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what a lament was. *Nasi'* follows the settled wording for Ezekiel ("prince" / "prince" / "ruler").

source.text: וְאָמַרְתָּ֗ מָ֤ה אִמְּךָ֙ לְבִיָּ֔א בֵּ֥ין אֲרָי֖וֹת רָבָ֑צָה בְּת֥וֹךְ כְּפִרִ֖ים רִבְּתָ֥ה גוּרֶֽיהָ׃

records.literal_gloss: and say: What [was] your mother? A lioness! Among lions she lay down; in the midst of young lions she reared her cubs.

en.L: and say: What [was] your mother? A lioness! \q Among lions she lay down; \q in the midst of young lions she reared her cubs.
en.B: and say: What a lioness your mother was! \q She lay down among lions; \q among young lions she reared her cubs.
en.R: Say this: Your mother was like a lioness! \q She lay down among the lions. \q She raised her cubs among the young lions.

decisions.choice: your mother, a lioness: the royal house of Judah, or the queen mother
alternatives: Hamutal, the mother of Jehoahaz and Zedekiah
decisions.reason: The lion was the emblem of Judah (Genesis 49:9). The "mother" may be Judah or Jerusalem, which bore its kings, or a particular queen mother. Hamutal was the mother of both Jehoahaz and Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:31; 24:18), and the queen mother had real power in Judah (Jeremiah 13:18). The text does not say.

decisions.choice: your mother: "your" is singular, addressed to the prince
decisions.reason: The lament speaks to one prince, perhaps the last king, Zedekiah, or to each prince in turn.

source.text: וַתַּ֛עַל אֶחָ֥ד מִגֻּרֶ֖יהָ כְּפִ֣יר הָיָ֑ה וַיִּלְמַ֥ד לִטְרָף־טֶ֖רֶף אָדָ֥ם אָכָֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And she brought up one of her cubs; a young lion he became, and he learned to tear prey; people he devoured.

en.L: And she raised up one of her cubs; a young lion he became, \q and he learned to tear prey; he devoured people.
en.B: She raised one of her cubs, and he became a young lion. \q He learned to tear prey, and he devoured people.
en.R: She raised one of her cubs, and he grew into a strong young lion. \q He learned to hunt, and he killed and ate people.

decisions.choice: one of her cubs: Jehoahaz, king of Judah in 609 BC
decisions.reason: Verse 4 says that this lion was taken to Egypt. That was the fate of Jehoahaz, son of Josiah, who reigned three months before Pharaoh Neco took him to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:31-34; Jeremiah 22:10-12, where he is called Shallum).

decisions.choice: he learned to tear prey; he devoured people: he became a strong and violent ruler
decisions.reason: The picture is of a lion that has learned to kill. It speaks of the young king's strength, and perhaps also of his cruelty (2 Kings 23:32).

source.text: וַיִּשְׁמְע֥וּ אֵלָ֛יו גּוֹיִ֖ם בְּשַׁחְתָּ֣ם נִתְפָּ֑שׂ וַיְבִאֻ֥הוּ בַֽחַחִ֖ים אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: And nations heard about him; in their pit he was caught, and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.

en.L: And nations heard about him; in their pit he was caught, \q and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.
en.B: The nations heard about him, and he was caught in their pit. \q They led him with hooks to the land of Egypt.
en.R: The nations heard about him, and they caught him in their pit. \q They put hooks in him and took him away to Egypt.

decisions.choice: caught in a pit, led with hooks: how lions were captured, and how captives were led away
decisions.reason: Lions were caught in pits dug as traps. Captives too were sometimes led with hooks or rings through the nose or jaw (2 Kings 19:28; 2 Chronicles 33:11).

source.text: וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ כִּ֣י נֽוֹחֲלָ֔ה אָבְדָ֖ה תִּקְוָתָ֑הּ וַתִּקַּ֛ח אֶחָ֥ד מִגֻּרֶ֖יהָ כְּפִ֥יר שָׂמָֽתְהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And she saw that she had waited, her hope was lost; and she took one of her cubs; a young lion she made him.

en.L: When she saw that she had waited, [that] her hope was lost, \q she took one of her cubs; a young lion she made him.
en.B: When she saw that she had waited in vain and her hope was gone, \q she took another of her cubs and made him into a young lion.
en.R: She waited, but she saw that there was no hope. \q So she took another of her cubs and made him a strong young lion.

decisions.choice: another of her cubs: a later king, probably Jehoiachin or Zedekiah
decisions.reason: This lion was taken to the king of Babylon (verse 9). That fits Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12-15), and also Zedekiah, taken there in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:6-7). Zedekiah had the same mother as Jehoahaz (verse 2), which would suit the picture of one mother; Jehoiachin's short reign and exile match the account of a lion taken in a net. The text does not name him.

decisions.choice: she had waited: she waited for the first cub to return, in vain
decisions.reason: The verb means to wait, and may also mean to be disappointed. Either way her hope for the first son ended.

source.text: וַיִּתְהַלֵּ֥ךְ בְּתוֹךְ־אֲרָי֖וֹת כְּפִ֣יר הָיָ֑ה וַיִּלְמַ֥ד לִטְרָף־טֶ֖רֶף אָדָ֥ם אָכָֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And he went about among lions; a young lion he became, and he learned to tear prey; people he devoured.

en.L: And he went about among lions; a young lion he became, \q and he learned to tear prey; he devoured people.
en.B: He prowled among the lions and became a young lion. \q He learned to tear prey, and he devoured people.
en.R: He prowled among the lions and grew into a strong young lion. \q He learned to hunt, and he killed and ate people.

decisions.choice: the wording of verse 3 at each level
decisions.reason: The second half of the verse repeats verse 3 word for word in Hebrew, and each level repeats its own wording of verse 3.

source.text: וַיֵּ֨דַע֙ אַלְמְנוֹתָ֔יו וְעָרֵיהֶ֖ם הֶחֱרִ֑יב וַתֵּ֤שַׁם אֶ֨רֶץ֙ וּמְלֹאָ֔הּ מִקּ֖וֹל שַׁאֲגָתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he knew his widows, and their cities he laid waste; and desolate was [the] land and its fullness from [the] sound of his roaring.

en.L: And he knew his widows \q and laid waste their cities, \q and the land and all that fills it was appalled \q at the sound of his roaring.
en.B: He preyed on their widows \q and laid waste their cities. \q The land and everything in it was appalled at the sound of his roaring.
en.R: He preyed on widows and destroyed their cities. \q Everyone in the land was terrified when they heard him roar.

decisions.choice: he knew his widows: an obscure phrase
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "he knew his widows", which is hard to understand in a picture of a lion. Changing one letter gives "he broke down their strongholds" (or "palaces"), which fits the next words, "laid waste their cities". The standard Hebrew text is kept here, understood as the lion preying on the helpless; it may also mean that he killed many men and so made their wives widows.

decisions.choice: the land was appalled at his roaring: the whole country lived in fear of him
decisions.reason: The roaring of the lion is the voice of a feared king (Proverbs 19:12; 20:2).

decisions.choice: preyed on
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense chosen in m1, which keeps to the lion picture.

source.text: וַיִּתְּנ֨וּ עָלָ֥יו גּוֹיִ֛ם סָבִ֖יב מִמְּדִינ֑וֹת וַֽיִּפְרְשׂ֥וּ עָלָ֛יו רִשְׁתָּ֖ם בְּשַׁחְתָּ֥ם נִתְפָּֽשׂ׃

records.literal_gloss: And nations set against him all around from [the] provinces, and they spread over him their net; in their pit he was caught.

en.L: Then nations set against him from the provinces all around, \q and they spread their net over him; in their pit he was caught.
en.B: Then nations from the provinces on every side set themselves against him. \q They spread their net over him, and he was caught in their pit.
en.R: Then the nations from all the lands around attacked him. \q They threw their net over him and caught him in their pit.

decisions.choice: nations from the provinces: the armies of the Babylonian empire
decisions.reason: Babylon's armies included troops from its subject peoples (2 Kings 24:2).

source.text: וַֽיִּתְּנֻ֤הוּ בַסּוּגַר֙ בַּֽחַחִ֔ים וַיְבִאֻ֖הוּ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ בָּבֶ֑ל יְבִאֻ֨הוּ֙ בַּמְּצֹד֔וֹת לְמַ֗עַן לֹא־יִשָּׁמַ֥ע קוֹל֛וֹ ע֖וֹד אֶל־הָרֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And they put him in a cage with hooks, and they brought him to [the] king of Babylon; they brought him into strongholds, so that his voice would not be heard again on [the] mountains of Israel.

en.L: And they put him with hooks into a cage \q and brought him to the king of Babylon; \q into strongholds they brought him, \q so that his voice would be heard no more on the mountains of Israel.
en.B: With hooks they put him in a cage \q and brought him to the king of Babylon. \q They put him in a stronghold, \q so that his roar would no longer be heard on the mountains of Israel.
en.R: They put him in a cage with hooks \q and took him to the king of Babylon. \q They locked him up, \q so that his roar would never again be heard on the mountains of Israel.

decisions.choice: strongholds: a prison, or hunting nets
decisions.reason: The word can mean strongholds or nets. Either way the lion is shut away and silenced.

decisions.choice: to the king of Babylon: the exile of Judah's king
decisions.reason: See the note at verse 5. Jehoiachin was kept in prison in Babylon for thirty-seven years (2 Kings 25:27).

source.text: אִמְּךָ֥ כַגֶּ֛פֶן בְּדָמְךָ֖ עַל־מַ֣יִם שְׁתוּלָ֑ה פֹּֽרִיָּה֙ וַֽעֲנֵפָ֔ה הָיְתָ֖ה מִמַּ֥יִם רַבִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Your mother [was] like a vine in your blood, by waters planted; fruitful and full of branches she was because of many waters.

en.L: Your mother [was] like a vine in your blood, planted by waters; \q fruitful and full of branches she was \q because of abundant waters.
en.B: Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted beside water. \q It bore fruit and was full of branches \q because there was plenty of water.
en.R: Your mother was like a grapevine in your blood, planted by the water. \q It had plenty of water, so it grew many branches and much fruit.

decisions.choice: in your blood: an obscure phrase, perhaps "of your own blood", that is, of your family
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "like a vine in your blood". It may mean that the prince comes from her blood, her family line. A small change to the text would give "like a vine in your vineyard" or "like a vine in your likeness". The standard Hebrew text is kept, and the phrase is left as it is at every level.

decisions.choice: your mother was like a vine: the royal house of Judah, pictured as in chapter 17
decisions.reason: The picture changes from the lioness to a vine, as in 17:6-8. The vine is the royal family, which once flourished.

decisions.choice: grapevine
decisions.reason: Readable says "grapevine" so that the reader pictures the right plant.

source.text: וַיִּֽהְיוּ־לָ֞הּ מַטּ֣וֹת עֹ֗ז אֶל־שִׁבְטֵי֙ מֹֽשְׁלִ֔ים וַתִּגְבַּ֥הּ קֽוֹמָת֖וֹ עַל־בֵּ֣ין עֲבֹתִ֑ים וַיֵּרָ֣א בְגָבְה֔וֹ בְּרֹ֖ב דָּלִיֹּתָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And there were to it strong branches for scepters of rulers, and its height towered among the thick branches, and it was seen in its height with the abundance of its branches.

en.L: And it had strong branches [fit] for scepters of rulers, \q and its height towered among the thick branches; \q and it was seen in its height, \q with the abundance of its branches.
en.B: Its branches were strong, fit to be rulers' scepters. \q It towered high above the thick branches; \q it stood out for its height \q and its many branches.
en.R: Its branches were strong, good for making rulers' scepters. \q It grew taller than all the branches around it. \q Everyone could see how tall it was \q and how many branches it had.

decisions.choice: strong branches for scepters of rulers: kings came from the royal line
decisions.reason: A scepter was a rod of rule. The vine's branches were strong enough to become rulers' rods: the line of David produced kings.

decisions.choice: thick branches: thick foliage, or the clouds
decisions.reason: The word can mean thick branches or clouds (compare 31:3). The vine towers high either way.

source.text: וַתֻּתַּ֤שׁ בְּחֵמָה֙ לָאָ֣רֶץ הֻשְׁלָ֔כָה וְר֥וּחַ הַקָּדִ֖ים הוֹבִ֣ישׁ פִּרְיָ֑הּ הִתְפָּרְק֧וּ וְיָבֵ֛שׁוּ מַטֵּ֥ה עֻזָּ֖הּ אֵ֥שׁ אֲכָלָֽתְהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: But it was plucked up in fury; to the ground it was thrown, and the east wind dried up its fruit; torn off and withered was its strong branch; fire consumed it.

en.L: But it was uprooted in wrath, to the ground it was cast down, \q and the east wind dried up its fruit; \q torn off and withered was its strong branch; fire consumed it.
en.B: But it was uprooted in wrath and thrown to the ground. \q The east wind dried up its fruit; \q its strong branch was broken off and withered, and fire consumed it.
en.R: But in anger it was pulled up and thrown on the ground. \q The hot east wind dried up its fruit. \q Its strong branch broke off and dried up, and fire burned it up.

decisions.choice: uprooted, withered, consumed: the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the kingdom
decisions.reason: The vine's end pictures the destruction of 586 BC, when the city fell and the last king was taken away. The east wind recalls the riddle of 17:10. "In wrath" (*chemah*) points to the LORD's anger as the cause.

decisions.choice: in wrath (L, B); in anger (R)
decisions.reason: The settled wording for *chemah* in Ezekiel, as published in chapters 1-7.

source.text: וְעַתָּ֖ה שְׁתוּלָ֣ה בַמִּדְבָּ֑ר בְּאֶ֖רֶץ צִיָּ֥ה וְצָמָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: And now [it is] planted in the wilderness, in a land of drought and thirst.

en.L: And now it is planted in the wilderness, \q in a land of drought and thirst.
en.B: Now it is planted in the desert, \q in a dry and thirsty land.
en.R: Now it is planted in the desert, \q in a dry land with no water.

decisions.choice: planted in the wilderness: the royal house in exile
decisions.reason: The vine that once grew by abundant water (verse 10) now stands in dry ground: the royal family and the people are in exile in Babylon.

source.text: וַתֵּצֵ֨א אֵ֜שׁ מִמַּטֵּ֤ה בַדֶּ֨יהָ֙ פִּרְיָ֣הּ אָכָ֔לָה וְלֹא־הָ֥יָה בָ֛הּ מַטֵּה־עֹ֖ז שֵׁ֣בֶט לִמְשׁ֑וֹל קִ֥ינָה הִ֖יא וַתְּהִ֥י לְקִינָֽה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And fire has gone out from [the] branch of its shoots; its fruit it has consumed, and there is not in it a strong branch, a scepter to rule. A lament it [is], and it has become a lament.

en.L: And fire has gone out from [one] branch of its shoots [and] consumed its fruit, \q and there is no strong branch left in it, a scepter to rule. \q This [is] a lament, and it has become a lament.
en.B: Fire has gone out from one of its branches and consumed its shoots and fruit. \q No strong branch is left on it, no scepter for ruling. \q This is a lament, and it has become a lament.
en.R: Fire spread from one of its own branches and burned up its shoots and its fruit. \q Now it has no strong branch left, no scepter for a king to rule with. \q This is a funeral song, and it is sung as a funeral song.

decisions.choice: fire went out from one of its branches: the royal house destroyed itself
decisions.reason: The fire comes from the vine itself. This probably points to Zedekiah, whose broken oath and revolt brought Babylon's army on Jerusalem (17:15-21).

decisions.choice: this is a lament, and it has become a lament: a closing note
decisions.reason: The last line steps outside the poem. It may mean that what was sung as a lament has now come true, or that it will be used as a lament from now on.

decisions.choice: funeral song; it is sung as a funeral song
decisions.reason: Readable uses "funeral song" for *qinah*, as in verse 1, and says that it is now in use.
